item.title: A New York City Comic Book Offers Tips on Rights and ICE Encounters
item.description:
As New York City middle school and high school students return to classrooms this term, they are receiving access to “Know Your Rights,” an educational comic book that prepares individuals for encounters with federal law enforcement officers.

It is the latest release by Civics for All, a program of the city schools’ department of social studies and civics. The program began in 2020 and now includes 45 comics. The print run of “Know Your Rights” is 140,000 — half in English, half in Spanish. It is also available digitally in 14 languages.

The comic presents vignettes, based on real events, about encounters with Immigration and Customs Enforcement, including guidance specific to New York City that emphasizes knowing your legal options at home, at work or walking to school. In easy-to-follow scenes with clear and brightly colored artwork, the story gives readers legal hotline numbers, and advice on planning ahead, organizing documents and memorizing emergency contact information.

“Know Your Rights,” written by Alex Segura and drawn by David Hahn, was suggested by members of Project Open Arms, a city school system effort to support immigrants, including asylum seekers. They saw value in helping students and families understand the rights that come with being an undocumented person.

The Education Department doesn’t track students’ and families’ immigration status but the number of students learning English in schools last year was about 146,000.

The comic arrives as the political climate around immigration remains heated. Last month, New York State’s Local Cops, Local Crimes Act went into effect. It bars ICE from deputizing local police to enforce civil immigration law. The publication also comes about six months after a high school student from the Bronx was freed from federal detention.

Earlier this month, Markwayne Mullin, the Homeland Security secretary, announced at a news conference that more than 2,000 people had recently been arrested by immigration officials in New York State in “Operation Rotten Apple.”

Speaking alongside Mullin, Kenneth Genalo, an ICE field office director for the city, invoked the attacks of Sept. 11 in his remarks, saying that “public safety depends on federal, state and local law enforcement cooperation.”

Using comics and graphic novels in schools is not new. “Maus,” by Art Spiegelman, in the 1990s “broke a lot of barriers in terms of the acceptance of comics,” Hillary Chute, an English professor at Northeastern University, who specializes in comics and graphic narratives, said in an interview. She was a graphic novels columnist for The New York Times Book Review from 2018 to 2022.

“In the past 10 years, there’s been a huge uptick in the pedagogical or instructional comics for kids,” she said, including a series of Science Comics published by First Second. She also is a fan of the Center for Cartoon Studies. “They’re part of that wave of thinking about instructional comics that really meets young people where they’re at.”

Jennifer Weber, a fellow specializing in education policy at the Manhattan Institute, the conservative think tank, said in an interview that using comics is not a bad thing, but that “Know Your Rights” portrays immigrants as the protagonists and ICE as the antagonists, which is “one-sided.”

For civics lessons, “I would say that you would absolutely need to understand the other side,” she continued, adding that the comic misses an opportunity to teach readers about why ICE was formed and to showcase Fourth Amendment protection from unreasonable searches and seizures.

Civics for All has published comics about government activism, Jackie Robinson, climate change, the 26th amendment and L.G.B.T.Q. figures.

Joe Schmidt, a senior instructional specialist in the social studies and civics department, said, “One of the things we have been able to do because we are not a traditional publisher is to be somewhat experimental” as long as the work prioritizes the “pedagogy and the needs of our students.” He and Brian Carlin, the department’s director of social studies and civics, founded the comics initiative.

One of Carlin’s goals has been to tell stories that receive little attention or are omitted from traditional historical narratives. “We did a story of the draft riots, you know, the largest riot in American history, and no one knows about it, and it happened here in New York” he said of the five days of rioting in 1863 by white workers angry about the Civil War military draft. The violent uprising left more than 100 dead.

Deciding which comics to produce is driven by gaps in curriculum content, Carlin said, or issues where there is a need for “another entry point to existing lessons.”

Segura said that writing this comic “felt really important,” adding that it provides valuable information “because we are experiencing a spike in activity from nonmunicipal law enforcement, namely ICE and organizations like that, where it’s imperative not only for kids, but their families and friends to know what their rights are and what the city can do to protect and help them.”

Politics aside, the aim of the comic is to inform. “People should know their rights, right?” Carlin asked. “That shouldn’t be controversial.”

item.title: The University of California Dumped the SAT. Let’s Not Bring It Back.
item.description:
When the University of California eliminated the SAT requirement for admission in 2021, U.C.L.A. saw a significant jump in applications from high-achieving Black and Latino students, for whom the standardized tests had been a barrier. “We are enrolling one of the most academically accomplished and diverse classes in our history,” the admissions director wrote. Since then, applications have risen at all nine undergraduate campuses, the most prestigious have become increasingly selective, and the university retains and graduates students at record rates.

Yet just five years later, the University of California is embroiled again in a very public battle over whether to reinstate the SAT. Faculty, whose 2020 recommendation to retain the test was overruled, have led the charge. In a widely circulated letter and opinion piece (both edited with the help of artificial intelligence), a math professor who organized the campaign blamed the test-blind admissions policy for a troubling increase in undergraduates who lack basic skills.

Math literacy is a real issue, not only in California, and not only since the elimination of the SAT for admissions. The argument that reinstituting the standardized test will rectify the math crisis, however, obscures a more fundamental debate over the mission of this elite public university and the longstanding tension between its twin goals of excellence and access.

The University of California is an educational juggernaut that has helped propel the state to its status as the world’s fourth-largest economy. It has arguably made its most important contribution not in Nobel Prizes, patents and scientific breakthroughs but in the lives of those not born into privilege. At a time of obscene wealth and inequality, that role has never been more important. The SAT fight is a proxy for a far more complex challenge: the university’s responsibility to remain true to its founding mission, crucial if the Golden State is to maintain its reputation as a land of opportunity and dreams.

To reinstate the SAT is to follow the pack rather than to lead, to grasp at a dubious shortcut rather than tackle more intractable underlying issues, chief among them the reality that the best public university in the country relies on one of the weakest, most inequitable public school systems.

California prides itself on setting trends. Its university, founded on a commitment to upward mobility for the working class, admitted women in 1870, pledged admission to all who qualified as part of a guarantee of universal access to higher education in 1960 and established scholarships for undocumented students in 2011.

The university has depended on high schools since its earliest years, when it began to accredit secondary schools and credentialed their teachers. Debates over ensuring equal access soon surfaced, though access was defined largely in terms of geographic barriers in such a large state. That began to change by the 1960s, as California became the most populous state, and then one of the most diverse.

The physics Nobel laureate Owen Chamberlain was among the first to raise concerns in the 1960s about the overwhelmingly white student body at Berkeley; he started a program where math and science faculty volunteered in local middle and high schools to coach both teachers and low-income students, who were predominantly Black and Mexican American. The program’s success led to some of the first educational opportunity programs, which targeted promising students who lacked the requisite grades or courses for admittance.

In the following decades, California’s school-age population became increasingly Latino, while gaps between the rich and the poor widened. Fallout from the infamous Prop 13 initiative of 1978, which cut and capped property taxes, exacerbated inequities among school districts. Numerous task force reports warned of a crisis as alarmingly few Black and Latino students, concentrated in schools with the poorest academic achievement, qualified for admission to the University of California. As demand for its most prestigious campuses far outstripped spots, affirmative action programs were blamed for excluding better-qualified students and then banned in 1995 by the Regents, the university’s governing board.

That action prompted the university to make a significant investment in improving K-12 education, in a quest to fulfill its promise to enroll a student population that mirrored the demographics of the state. At its height, before budget crises sapped the initiative, the university spent more than $300 million annually on professional development programs and partnerships with dozens of middle and high schools to increase the percentage of underrepresented students who qualified for admission.

Karl Pister, an engineer who oversaw the outreach, lamented that among the university’s three missions — research, education and service — service was consistently given the least attention. As he wrote prophetically in 1998: “If we don’t improve our schools, our children and grandchildren will live in a world divided — an angry world of haves and have-nots, of those who can analyze and synthesize information to meet new challenges and those who cannot.”

That angry world today compels the University of California to define its responsibility to K-12 education with a long-term commitment that goes beyond harvesting the best and brightest in a troubled system. The university needs to conceptualize a master plan for the 21st century that evokes the spirit of Mr. Pister, re-emphasizes the service mission and applies the institution’s vast resources to grapple with the reality of public schools in a state where two-thirds of students enter high school without proficiency in grade-level math. Otherwise, the university will continue to rely on patchwork fixes to cope with the glaring disparities among high schools and corresponding inequities in the education available to different groups.

Arguments over the value of the SAT have been litigated and re-litigated since the Regents elevated its importance in admissions by a one-vote margin in 1977. Even its advocates point to studies that show the test has predictive value of success only largely for freshman year. Under the university’s unusual shared governance structure, a faculty committee will issue recommendations by June 2027; final action will be up to the Regents, who have already expanded the discussion to look broadly at college readiness.

What has made the University of California exceptional is its commitment to increase access without sacrificing excellence. In recent years, California has proudly defied a national trend: On average, about 40 percent of its students are the first in their families to attend a four-year college. More than half qualify for free tuition. The percentages of underrepresented students have crept up, through a variety of initiatives. The California Dream Act gave undocumented students access to financial aid, as well as in-state tuition. Students on University of California campuses may struggle with basic math, but they are graduating at record rates.

These are perilous times for the very students for whom the University of California is a life-changing experience. Cuts in federal aid have reduced support programs, especially vital for first-generation students. ICE raids mean even citizens fear filling out financial aid forms that might jeopardize their undocumented relatives. International students face restrictions on visas.

The University of California needs to redouble its commitment to forge its own path, to remain a beacon of hope, albeit flickering. Now is not the moment to regress.

Miriam Pawel is the author of the forthcoming “California Dreams: The Making and Remaking of the University of California.”

item.title: California Sets Standards for Homes Tainted by Wildfire Smoke
item.description:
Gov. Gavin Newsom of California signed legislation on Tuesday establishing what supporters say is the country’s first science-based standard for determining when a home impacted by a wildfire is safe to occupy.

The legislation addresses a basic question that has become the source of a protracted dispute between insurance companies and homeowners after the January 2025 Eaton and Palisades fires: How clean is clean enough?

Until now, California had no uniform, statewide standard for determining when a smoke-contaminated home was safe for a family to reoccupy. In that vacuum, homeowners and their insurers battled over what contaminants they should test for, what levels were considered dangerous and how extensively a house needed to be cleaned.

Assembly Bill 1642 places those determinations in the hands of the state’s health and environmental agencies.

“Science, not an insurance company’s opinions, will determine whether a home is safe,” said California Assemblymember John Harabedian, the author of the bill, in a statement. His district includes the community of Altadena, where thousands of standing homes were impacted by toxic smoke and many remain unoccupied.

AB 1642 gives the California Department of Toxic Substances Control two years to develop standards for testing and removing contaminants carried by smoke. The list of contaminants that will be addressed by the new law include the so-called CAM-17 panel, which includes heavy metals like beryllium and lead. Separately, the law calls for testing other toxins like cyanide, manganese and lithium.

“Up until this bill was signed, there were no objective standards based on science,” said Mr. Harabedian in an interview, adding that the bill was in part catalyzed by investigations by The New York Times which shed light on the extent of the contamination and the impact on public health.

The law, which was sponsored by Eaton Fire Residents United — a community group that emerged in Altadena when homeowners met and began posting their lab tests showing contamination from the smoke — dovetails with AB 1795, which was also signed by Mr. Newsom on Tuesday.

Whereas AB 1642 requires the state to create the standard for each contaminant and requires that homes exposed to wildfire smoke be tested both before and after remediation, AB 1795 lays out how insurers will need to address smoke contamination. Going forward, insurers will be required to pay for testing and they will not be allowed to end payments for a policyholder’s rental unit and other additional living expenses until the home has been restored and is deemed safe to occupy.

Both bills state that if debris from the fire is found inside a home within the perimeter of the wildfire impact zone, then it is presumed to be a result of the fire. Following the Los Angeles fires, insurers routinely argued that contaminants found inside the home predated the blaze.

The insurance industry opposed the bills “vigorously,” said Mr. Harabedian.

In an email, Nicole Ganley, the assistant vice president for public affairs of the American Property Casualty Insurance Association, a trade group representing the insurance industry, said that the group had “opposed both bills as introduced because they contained provisions that raised significant concerns regarding cost, implementation, and consistency with established smoke-testing and remediation practices.”

Dr. Francois Tissot, an isotope geochemist at the California Institute of Technology, whose own home in Altadena was contaminated by smoke and who remains displaced, said that the two bills will go a long way to addressing the systemic issues faced by homeowners like him.

“First, it makes it mandatory for insurers to test for contaminants. This seems obvious but a lot of families had to fight to even get simple testing done,” said Dr. Tissot, who was part of the working group that finessed the language in each bill. “Second, if contaminants are found, it creates the presumption that they come from the fire — no more excuses from insurers such as, ‘You have a fireplace and use candles,’” he wrote in a text exchange.

Legislators said that they are hopeful that these bills could set the stage for nationwide change. Together, they address what Dr. Tissot describes as a “curse in disguise” — the experience of having your home survive a historic fire only to realize that you might have been better off if your home had burned to the ground.

“Families look like they avoided the worst, they haven’t lost their homes to the flames. And yet they need to discard their belongings, their home is unsafe, and they have to fight to even have their loss be even recognized, let alone addressed properly,” he said.
